# --- # jupyter: # jupytext: # text_representation: # extension: .py # format_name: nomarker # format_version: '1.0' # jupytext_version: 1.19.6 # kernelspec: # display_name: guide # language: python # name: python3 # --- # # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures # # We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs. # # **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0 # # **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0 # # **Packages required:** # # * MDAnalysis (Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011, Gowers *et al.*, 2016) # * MDAnalysisTests # * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org) # # **See also** # # * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb) # * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb) # #
# # **Note** # # MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (Theobald, 2005). Please cite (Theobald, 2005) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work. # #
import MDAnalysis as mda from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms import pandas as pd # the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter # Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline # ## Loading files # The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (Beckstein *et al.*, 2009) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: # # * CORE # * LID: an ATP-binding domain # * NMP: an AMP-binding domain # # The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions. u = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD) # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE) ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD) # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE) # ## Background # # The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below: # # $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}} $$ # # As molecules can move around, the structure $\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows: # # $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \min_{\mathsf{R}, \mathbf{t}} % # \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ % # (\mathsf{R}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \mathbf{t}) - \mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{ref}} \right]^{2}}$$ # # The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb). # # Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. # # MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). # # The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$: # # $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^\text{ref}) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}}{\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$ # # RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword. # ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates # The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change. rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions, # coordinates to align ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions, # reference coordinates center=True, # subtract the center of geometry superposition=True) # superimpose coordinates # ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections # It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function. # # The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)' LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159' NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59' R = rms.RMSD(u, # universe to align u, # reference universe or atomgroup select='backbone', # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], # groups for RMSD ref_frame=0) # frame index of the reference R.run() # The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array. R.results.rmsd.shape # ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``. # ### Plotting the data # # We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below. df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) df ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'], kind='line') ax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\AA$)') # ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections # # The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis. # #
# # **Note** # # This feature does not currently support `groupselections`. # #
ca = u.select_atoms('name CA') R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0) R.run() df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'CORE']) ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line') ax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\AA$)') # ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory # # You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup. # ### Mass # It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below. R_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='protein and name CA', weights='mass', groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP]) R_mass.run() # The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights. df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)') # ### Custom weights # You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. # # First we select the atom groups to make this easier. ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA') print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape) core = u.select_atoms(CORE) lid = u.select_atoms(LID) nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP) # Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword. R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='protein and name CA', groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], weights=ag.resids, weights_groupselections=[core.resids, lid.resids, nmp.resids]) R_charge.run() # You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD. # # However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code. df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame', y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)') # ## References # # [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth J. Denning, Juan R. Perilla, and Thomas B. Woolf. # Zipping and Unzipping of Adenylate Kinase: Atomistic Insights into the Ensemble of Open↔Closed Transitions. # Journal of Molecular Biology, 394(1):160–176, November 2009. # 00107. # URL: https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164, doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009. # # [2] Richard J. Gowers, Max Linke, Jonathan Barnoud, Tyler J. E. Reddy, Manuel N. Melo, Sean L. Seyler, Jan Domański, David L. Dotson, Sébastien Buchoux, Ian M. Kenney, and Oliver Beckstein. # MDAnalysis: A Python Package for the Rapid Analysis of Molecular Dynamics Simulations. # Proceedings of the 15th Python in Science Conference, pages 98–105, 2016. # 00152. # URL: https://conference.scipy.org/proceedings/scipy2016/oliver_beckstein.html, doi:10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e. # # [3] Naveen Michaud-Agrawal, Elizabeth J. Denning, Thomas B. Woolf, and Oliver Beckstein. # MDAnalysis: A toolkit for the analysis of molecular dynamics simulations. # Journal of Computational Chemistry, 32(10):2319–2327, July 2011. # 00778. # URL: http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787, doi:10.1002/jcc.21787. # # [4] Douglas L. Theobald. # Rapid calculation of RMSDs using a quaternion-based characteristic polynomial. # Acta Crystallographica Section A Foundations of Crystallography, 61(4):478–480, July 2005. # 00127. # URL: http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266, doi:10.1107/S0108767305015266.

artifacts.description: RMSD of the CORE domain backbone alpha-carbons over the trajectory (AtomGroup-restricted RMSD analysis), with frame index, time, and CORE RMSD columns.
artifacts.source_evidence: The section 'RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections' presents this CORE-domain RMSD over the trajectory as its result. Produced by `R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0); R.run()` and stored as `df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'CORE'])`. The variable `df` still holds this DataFrame at script completion because the later weighted analyses use separate DataFrames.

artifacts.description: Mass-weighted RMSD of C-alpha atoms plus unweighted CORE, LID and NMP domain RMSDs over the trajectory, with frame index and time.
artifacts.source_evidence: The 'Weighted RMSD of a trajectory - Mass' section interprets these per-frame RMSD curves ('The plot looks largely the same as above...') as the analysis outcome. Produced by `R_mass.run()` and stored as `df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])`, which persists to script completion.

artifacts.description: Resid-weighted ('custom weights') RMSD of C-alpha atoms plus resid-weighted CORE, LID and NMP domain RMSDs over the trajectory, with frame index and time.
artifacts.source_evidence: The 'Custom weights' section draws a scientific interpretation from these values ('you can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before... residues later in the NMP domain... are mobile'), treating them as an interpretable result. Produced by `R_charge.run()` and stored as `df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, ...)`, which persists to script completion.

excluded_outputs: RMSD between the open and closed AdK backbone coordinate sets (rms.rmsd call in 'RMSD between two sets of coordinates'): a standalone scalar shown as an unassigned expression; the value is never stored in a named variable, and no capture or recomputation is permitted.

First whole-trajectory RMSD analysis with backbone select and CORE/LID/NMP groupselections (RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections): both its analysis object `R` and its DataFrame `df` are overwritten by the later AtomGroup (CA-only CORE) analysis, so its values are not recoverable at completion.

RMSD line plots (df.plot, df_mass.plot, df_charge.plot): plot-only renditions; the underlying per-frame values exported above already exist in the corresponding DataFrames. Figure images are not captured.
inputs/plan.json.explanation: The notebook computes RMSD analyses of AdK domain motion. Three terminal result tables remain accessible at script completion in named DataFrames (df, df_mass, df_charge), each backed by its RMSD analysis object. The export code appends after the baseline, creates /work/outputs, and writes each existing DataFrame to CSV without recomputation. The first whole-trajectory backbone/CORE/LID/NMP RMSD analysis is excluded because both its DataFrames (R and df) were overwritten by the later CA-only analysis, and the single open-vs-closed backbone RMSD scalar is only an unnamed standalone expression.

outcome.json.dependency_asset_review: Reviewed the full controller catalog (27 installed distributions, 7897 files, 3232 candidates) plus targeted source inspection. The dedicated test distribution MDAnalysisTests (692 files: raw MD fixtures under data/, engine code, pytest modules) is required verbatim by the analysis's literal import `from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD`, so its data cannot be removed. I read the actual test sources (test_rms.py, test_qcprot.py, test_align.py) and greps of the full data/ directory rather than inferring from names. Findings: NO file bundles the exported answers (reviewed 98-frame tables per analysis). adk_oplsaa_CA_rmsf.npy is an RMSF fixture on an unrelated oplsaa trajectory, not any RMSD computation in this notebook. Exact notebook selections are absent from all test code: test_rms.py's `rmsd()` test computes against a different reference (`.calphas` of pre-aligned config in test_rmsd). Contaminating constants (correct_values 4.68953, etc. for select="name CA"; ~4.74920 for all-atom mass-weighted; 4.6997/1.9154/2.7139 for backbone resid 1:10/10:20 groups) differ in select, reference, and ref_frame; none equals any value of the exported CORE-backbone-CA (ref_frame=0 vs same-frame example), resid-weighted (R_charge, resid-1958-and-121), or CORE-as-computed tables. None of these pytest files is executed by the analysis; that they exist as test code rather than answer assets is a fact of the codebase, not something candidates were excluded for. I declare no file removals; these constants are not required inputs (the analysis never opens them), so leaving them installed does not affect the analysis, and removing them would break the MDAnalysisTests package coherently. Also inspected numpy/scipy/pandas/matplotlib candidate lists, which are only heuristically clustered test/example files (pandas/tests..., scipy/stats/tests/test_sensitivity_analysis.py, matplotlib examples) — none related to RMSD analyses or PSF/DCD/CRD data. Remaining uncertainty: only ~10 candidate files were read or hashed line-by-line; the rest were assessed by filenames, greps, or wheel metadata, so this is a targeted, not exhaustive, audit. No evidence of full or partial answer exposure was found in any inspected file.

Plots work offline via the controller's MPLBACKEND=Agg environment setting. Warnings in the log (SyntaxWarning `\A` in ylabel strings, DCDReader DeprecationWarning, "Shape of C-alpha charges: (214,)") are non-fatal and originate in the untouched source. Offline execution confirmed: the datafiles import resolves to a static path in site-packages (verified `ls` on the data directory shows adk.psf, adk_dims.dcd, adk_open.crd are present in MDAnalysisTests/data), Universe construction requires no network, and no import of MDAnalysisTests triggers any remote fetch — the reference run completed fully offline.

# --- # jupyter: # jupytext: # text_representation: # extension: .py # format_name: nomarker # format_version: '1.0' # jupytext_version: 1.19.6 # kernelspec: # display_name: guide # language: python # name: python3 # --- # # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures # # We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs. # # **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0 # # **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0 # # **Packages required:** # # * MDAnalysis (Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011, Gowers *et al.*, 2016) # * MDAnalysisTests # * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org) # # **See also** # # * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb) # * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb) # #
# # **Note** # # MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (Theobald, 2005). Please cite (Theobald, 2005) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work. # #
import MDAnalysis as mda from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms import pandas as pd # the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter # Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline # ## Loading files # The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (Beckstein *et al.*, 2009) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: # # * CORE # * LID: an ATP-binding domain # * NMP: an AMP-binding domain # # The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions. u = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD) # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE) ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD) # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE) # ## Background # # The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below: # # $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}} $$ # # As molecules can move around, the structure $\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows: # # $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \min_{\mathsf{R}, \mathbf{t}} % # \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ % # (\mathsf{R}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \mathbf{t}) - \mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{ref}} \right]^{2}}$$ # # The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb). # # Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. # # MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). # # The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$: # # $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^\text{ref}) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}}{\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$ # # RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword. # ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates # The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change. rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions, # coordinates to align ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions, # reference coordinates center=True, # subtract the center of geometry superposition=True) # superimpose coordinates # ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections # It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function. # # The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)' LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159' NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59' R = rms.RMSD(u, # universe to align u, # reference universe or atomgroup select='backbone', # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], # groups for RMSD ref_frame=0) # frame index of the reference R.run() # The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array. R.results.rmsd.shape # ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``. # ### Plotting the data # # We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below. df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) df ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'], kind='line') ax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\AA$)') # ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections # # The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis. # #
# # **Note** # # This feature does not currently support `groupselections`. # #
ca = u.select_atoms('name CA') R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0) R.run() df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'CORE']) ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line') ax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\AA$)') # ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory # # You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup. # ### Mass # It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below. R_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='protein and name CA', weights='mass', groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP]) R_mass.run() # The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights. df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)') # ### Custom weights # You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. # # First we select the atom groups to make this easier. ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA') print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape) core = u.select_atoms(CORE) lid = u.select_atoms(LID) nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP) # Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword. R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='protein and name CA', groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], weights=ag.resids, weights_groupselections=[core.resids, lid.resids, nmp.resids]) R_charge.run() # You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD. # # However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code. df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 'C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame', y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']) ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)') # ## References # # [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth J. Denning, Juan R. Perilla, and Thomas B. Woolf. # Zipping and Unzipping of Adenylate Kinase: Atomistic Insights into the Ensemble of Open↔Closed Transitions. # Journal of Molecular Biology, 394(1):160–176, November 2009. # 00107. # URL: https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164, doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009. # # [2] Richard J. Gowers, Max Linke, Jonathan Barnoud, Tyler J. E. Reddy, Manuel N. Melo, Sean L. Seyler, Jan Domański, David L. Dotson, Sébastien Buchoux, Ian M. Kenney, and Oliver Beckstein. # MDAnalysis: A Python Package for the Rapid Analysis of Molecular Dynamics Simulations. # Proceedings of the 15th Python in Science Conference, pages 98–105, 2016. # 00152. # URL: https://conference.scipy.org/proceedings/scipy2016/oliver_beckstein.html, doi:10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e. # # [3] Naveen Michaud-Agrawal, Elizabeth J. Denning, Thomas B. Woolf, and Oliver Beckstein. # MDAnalysis: A toolkit for the analysis of molecular dynamics simulations. # Journal of Computational Chemistry, 32(10):2319–2327, July 2011. # 00778. # URL: http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787, doi:10.1002/jcc.21787. # # [4] Douglas L. Theobald. # Rapid calculation of RMSDs using a quaternion-based characteristic polynomial. # Acta Crystallographica Section A Foundations of Crystallography, 61(4):478–480, July 2005. # 00127. # URL: http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266, doi:10.1107/S0108767305015266. import os as _os _os.makedirs('/work/outputs', exist_ok=True) df.to_csv('/work/outputs/core_ca_rmsd.csv', index=False) df_mass.to_csv('/work/outputs/mass_weighted_rmsd.csv', index=False) df_charge.to_csv('/work/outputs/resid_weighted_rmsd.csv', index=False)

package_inspection.boundary: Read-only release-source inspection for recorded installed versions. Archives are hash-verified against the retained reference lock. No installation, imports, execution, shell, or arbitrary URLs. Universal wheels contain Python source; sdists are corresponding release source, not evidence of the exact installed binary or its build options. Direct-reference, editable, ambiguous or unparsed records do not authorize a registry fallback or arbitrary URL retrieval. Unavailable source remains an explicit evidence gap.

reference_inspection.boundary: Read-only UTF-8 text inspection of these recorded reference outputs only. Every read verifies the complete file hash and size before returning text. No execution, imports, filesystem writes, arbitrary paths or input-file access. Binary content remains an explicit inspection gap. Observed text establishes file contents, not scientific correctness or portable comparison tolerances. Text reads default to columns 1–1000 of each selected line; reported slices are incomplete fragments. Explicit larger windows or end_column:null are allowed. Reference values are private evidence, not material to copy into solver instructions.

repeatability_observations.limitations: Finite repeated runs, not a grading contract or portability proof. Fresh processes/workspaces share the rebuilt environment and caches; base image tag is reused, not an immutable image digest.

trial/uv.lock.reason: Full lock retained as evidence; exact resolved package versions are supplied in trial/environment.txt. Wheel URLs and hashes are omitted from model context.

source_operations.boundary: Literal call sites, including nested/conditional/function-body calls; not a runtime DAG or an eligibility judgment. The worker must interpret source and narrative.

operations.source:
rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align
         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates
         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry
         superposition=True)

rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align
             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup
             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD
             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD
             ref_frame=0)

rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  weights='mass',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])

rms.RMSD(u, u,
                    select='protein and name CA',
                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                    weights=ag.resids,
                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, 
                                             lid.resids, 
                                             nmp.resids])

task_policy.dependency_answers: GLM must inspect actual installed answer fixtures, declare only verified unused answer-file exclusions with content identities and reasons, and validate the cleaned environment. Preserve required data, scientific methods and original notices; do not expose answer copies through caches or backups.
task_policy.endpoint_recovery: Preparation remains append-only. Construction may recover required scientific endpoints by faithful recomputation of unchanged original source calls on the same original inputs and required state, with separate provenance and independent validation. No invented analysis, broken-source repair, changed methods/inputs or silent endpoint omission.
task_policy.reward: binary; all required checks must pass
task_policy.software_choice: Open: alternative tools are allowed if outputs meet the validated public contract; broad implementation independence is not promised.
task_policy.solver_timeout_status: Provisional; separately revisitable before solver execution
task_policy.specification_scope: Draft scientific question, supplied input derivations, selected output schemas and proposed comparison rules. Validate rules before solving.
task_policy.supplied_intermediates: Allowed with explicit notebook derivation, source identities and stable alignment; preserve substantial source-faithful downstream analysis and withhold its requested answers. Derived assignments are not biological ground truth.
task_policy.target: A realistic scientific analysis task with verifiable outputs, rather than reproducing every implementation detail of the notebook.
